questions.stem: A technician wants to see which ports a Windows server is listening on right now, from the server itself, without scanning it over the network. Which command BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: a local view of listening ports and connections.
A scan, which is what the technician wants to avoid.

questions.explanation: netstat shows active connections, listening ports, routing table, and interface statistics on the local host (netstat -an). It is a local view; nmap probes hosts over the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: netstat: local view of what is connected or listening.

questions.stem: A technician runs the command below. What does the output BEST show?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> nslookup intranet.corp.example.com
Server:   dns1.corp.example.com
Address:  10.1.9.53

*** dns1.corp.example.com can't find intranet.corp.example.com: Non-existent domain

options.text: The DNS server has no record for that name
options.rationale: Correct: the server answered, saying the name doesn't exist.

options.text: The lookup for the intranet failed
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: The intranet web server is down
options.rationale: DNS says nothing about the web server's state.

options.text: The PC has no route to its DNS server
options.rationale: dns1 replied, so the PC reached it.

questions.explanation: nslookup queries DNS to resolve names to IPs and back. It is the basic DNS troubleshooting tool on Windows and Linux; 'Non-existent domain' means the server answered that the name isn't in DNS.
questions.discriminator_tested: nslookup: basic DNS troubleshooting.

questions.stem: Compared with nslookup, what BEST describes the extra value of dig?

options.text: Record sections, TTLs, and query time
options.rationale: Correct: much more detail about the answer.

options.text: It runs on Linux and macOS
options.rationale: True, but platform isn't added value.

options.text: It traces each router hop to the server
It captures DNS packets on the wire

questions.explanation: dig is a detailed DNS query tool (dig example.com MX). It is more detailed than nslookup, showing record sections, TTL, and query time.
questions.discriminator_tested: dig is more detailed than nslookup.

questions.stem: A technician runs the tests below. Which conclusion is BEST supported?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> ping 10.1.9.15
Reply from 10.1.9.15: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=128
Reply from 10.1.9.15: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=128

C:\> ping 10.1.9.16
Request timed out.
Request timed out.

options.text: .15 answers; .16 is down or filtering ICMP
options.rationale: Correct: silence from .16 has more than one cause.
True, but it says nothing about .16.
A failed ping doesn't prove the host is down.

questions.explanation: ping tests reachability and round-trip time with ICMP echo. A failed ping doesn't prove the host is down, because ICMP may be blocked.
questions.discriminator_tested: A failed ping does not prove the host is down.

questions.stem: What does tracert reveal that ping doesn't?

options.text: Where on the path it fails
options.rationale: Correct: it lists each hop up to the failure.

options.text: Which ports are open on each router

questions.explanation: tracert (Windows) or traceroute (Linux/macOS) shows each hop along the path to a destination. It locates where along the path connectivity fails.
questions.discriminator_tested: tracert locates where along the path connectivity fails.

questions.stem: Which two tasks need a packet capture tool such as tcpdump rather than netstat? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reading the contents of DNS queries
Seeing each packet of a TCP handshake
Showing established connections and their PIDs

questions.explanation: tcpdump is command-line packet capture and analysis. It captures actual packets; netstat only lists connections.
questions.discriminator_tested: tcpdump captures packets; netstat lists connections.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes nmap from netstat?

options.text: nmap probes other hosts; netstat, the local one

options.rationale: True, but not the fundamental difference.

options.text: netstat probes other hosts; nmap reports the local one

questions.explanation: nmap scans hosts for live devices, open ports, services, and OS details; it probes other hosts. netstat reports on the local host.
questions.discriminator_tested: nmap probes other hosts; netstat reports the local host.

questions.stem: A screen-lock setting isn't taking effect on a PC. The output below is from that PC. What BEST explains why?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> gpresult /r
COMPUTER SETTINGS
    Applied Group Policy Objects
        Default Domain Policy
        Workstation Baseline
    The following GPOs were not applied because they were filtered out
        Screen Lock Policy
            Filtering:  Denied (Security)

options.rationale: Correct: the GPO was filtered out by its security filtering.

options.text: The Screen Lock Policy wasn't applied
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: The Default Domain Policy overrides it
options.rationale: The output shows filtering, not an override.

options.text: The PC has lost contact with the domain
options.rationale: Other GPOs applied, so it reached the domain.

questions.explanation: gpresult shows the Group Policy settings applied to a user or computer (gpresult /r). It is Windows-only and confirms which policies actually applied, and why others didn't.
questions.discriminator_tested: gpresult confirms which policies actually applied.

questions.stem: A port scan of a server returns the lines below. What does 'filtered' on port 443 MOST likely mean?
questions.exhibit:
PORT      STATE     SERVICE
22/tcp    open      ssh
80/tcp    closed    http
443/tcp   filtered  https

options.text: A firewall likely dropped the probe
options.rationale: Correct: no answer came back, typical of a firewall.

options.text: The scanner got no clear answer from 443
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say the likely reason.

options.text: HTTPS is listening and accepting connections
The host refused the connection with a reset

questions.explanation: A port scanner probes a host to find open, closed, or filtered ports. Filtered means the probe got no clear answer, usually because a firewall dropped it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Port scanner reports open, closed, or filtered.

questions.stem: A security team runs iPerf against a server, expecting it to list the server's open ports. What is the MAIN problem?

options.text: iPerf measures throughput, not open ports
iPerf needs a server running at the far end
options.rationale: True, but even then it wouldn't list ports.

options.text: iPerf scans one port at a time
options.rationale: iPerf doesn't scan ports at all.

questions.explanation: iPerf measures network throughput between two endpoints (client and server, TCP or UDP). It is performance testing, not security scanning.
questions.discriminator_tested: iPerf is performance testing, not security scanning.

questions.stem: A ping sweep of a user subnet returns the results below. What is the BEST next step for 10.1.4.88?
questions.exhibit:
IP scan 10.1.4.0/24 (ping sweep)
10.1.4.1    00:1a:2b:3c:4d:01   Cisco Systems      (gateway, in inventory)
10.1.4.20   3c:52:82:aa:10:7e   Dell               (LT-0112, in inventory)
10.1.4.88   b8:27:eb:5f:22:91   Raspberry Pi Fdn   (not in inventory)

options.rationale: Correct: an unknown device on a user subnet needs checking.

options.text: Add it to the hardware inventory
options.rationale: Premature: first find out what it is and whether it belongs.

options.text: Run iPerf against it to test its speed
Ignore it, since it answered the ping
options.rationale: Answering a ping doesn't make it authorized.

questions.explanation: An IP scanner discovers active devices across an address range (a ping sweep). It answers 'which hosts are on this network?' and finds rogue devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: IP scanner finds rogue devices.

questions.stem: Which two fields belong in a hardware inventory record? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: That belongs in the software inventory.
A scan result, not an inventory field.

questions.explanation: A hardware inventory records physical devices: type, serial, owner, location, and status. You can't protect devices you don't know exist.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hardware inventory: type, serial, owner, location, status.

questions.stem: IT needs one place to track each laptop from purchase, through assignment and repairs, to secure disposal. What BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: the system of record for the whole lifecycle.
Tags identify devices but hold no history.
Tracks installed software, not device lifecycles.

questions.explanation: Asset management systems track assets from purchase through disposal; they are the system of record. A tag is only the physical identifier.
questions.discriminator_tested: Asset management system = system of record.

questions.stem: Which statement about asset tags is BEST?

options.rationale: Correct: they tie the physical device to its inventory record.

options.text: They carry a unique ID, often as a barcode
options.rationale: True, but the purpose is linking the device to its record.

options.text: They store the device's full history
options.rationale: The asset management system holds the history.

questions.explanation: An asset tag is a physical, barcode, or RFID label with a unique ID on a device. It ties the physical device to its inventory record.
questions.discriminator_tested: Asset tag ties the device to its record.

questions.stem: Which two problems can a software inventory reveal? (Choose two.)

options.text: Unknown devices plugged into the network
options.rationale: An IP scan or hardware inventory finds those.

questions.explanation: A software inventory records installed software, versions, and licenses. Versions reveal vulnerable software, and the inventory also flags unauthorized or unlicensed programs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Versions reveal vulnerable software; flags unlicensed programs.

questions.stem: Which two actions are remediation? (Choose two.)

options.text: Isolating a device that can't be fixed

questions.explanation: Remediation means fixing or mitigating identified vulnerabilities and non-compliance: patch, reconfigure, remove, or isolate. Discovery alone fixes nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Remediation acts on findings.

questions.stem: A patch broke a payroll application, and IT couldn't undo it for two days. Which remediation consideration was MOST clearly missing?

options.rationale: Correct: the inability to undo is the failure described.
Also important, but the two days of no undo point to rollback.
More time wouldn't have given a way back.

questions.explanation: Remediation considerations weigh risk and priority, business impact, testing, maintenance windows, dependencies, and a rollback plan.
questions.discriminator_tested: Keep a rollback plan.

questions.stem: Policy requires proof that every retired drive was sanitized. What should the disposal process BEST include to satisfy this?

options.text: Sanitizing each drive before it leaves
options.rationale: Necessary, but without a record there's no proof.

options.text: A verbal sign-off from the technician
Deleting the files on each drive

questions.explanation: Destruction and disposal means retiring devices and media so data can't be recovered, following policy and documenting it. Deleting files isn't sanitizing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Follow policy and document it.

questions.stem: A drive is given a quick standard format before being resold. What can a buyer MOST likely do?

options.text: Recover much of the old data
options.rationale: Correct: a standard format leaves the data in place.
True, but it misses the risk.

options.text: Nothing; the format erased the data
options.rationale: A standard format rebuilds structures; the data remains.

questions.explanation: A standard format rebuilds file system structures; a low-level format overwrites every sector. A standard format leaves data recoverable.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard format leaves data recoverable.

questions.stem: Hard drives from a call center will be reused internally. Which method BEST balances security and reuse?

options.rationale: Correct: unrecoverable data, and the drives stay usable.

questions.explanation: Hard drive sanitization makes data unrecoverable; the method depends on sensitivity and whether the drive will be reused. Reuse allows overwrite or wipe.
questions.discriminator_tested: Reuse allows overwrite or wipe.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why an overwrite is usually fine for a working hard disk but questionable for an SSD?

options.text: SSDs remap cells the overwrite may not reach
options.rationale: Correct: wear levelling leaves data in cells outside the addressable space.

options.text: SSDs store data differently from HDDs
options.rationale: True, but vague; it doesn't say what defeats the overwrite.

questions.explanation: Overwrite writes patterns over all addressable areas in one or more passes. It allows reuse but is less reliable on SSDs and failed sectors.
questions.discriminator_tested: Overwrite is less reliable on SSDs.
